title: Joe Turner's 'The Boss of the Blues' session with Kansas City veterans
summary: Called to a Carnegie Hall rehearsal-room date, Leeman finds Joe Turner, Pete Johnson, Pete Brown, Lawrence Brown and Freddie Green, the only white player, in a record later ranked among the best.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: My first record date: sessions, personnel, discography

blocks.x: I've got to get to one of the most exciting record dates, and a definite high point in my career. I was called by -- I don't remember whom, to do a record date while I was on the Hit Parade, and I had a record in front of me, and if you wait until I research, I'll give you the year.

Well, there is no date on the album, but I think it was around '55. I was called for a record date at Carnegie Hall rehearsal hall, that's where it took place and they had set up equipment there, and when I walked in, I was flabbergasted the people on the date. In the first place, I walked in - and I always walk in early to set up the drums; there was Walter Pope there, and we said greetings and Joe Newman was there, and we had just begun to know each other, really; and Lawrence Brown on trombone; Pete Brown on alto sax -- now he'd been ill, and they found him. He hadn't played for a couple of years, and Frank Wes$ on tenor saxophone, and Pete Johnson on piano. Now the last time I saw or heard about Pete was at the Sunset Club, which we covered back in Kansas City in 1935, and all these people were in Kansas City in 1935. Freddie Greene was there on guitar, and
I was the only white on the date, and this was -- well, the date was Joe Turner's, and the name of the album, which is a collector's item, is The Boss of the Blues.

I think he had asked for all the musicians that they could reproduce from the old days in Kansas City in that association, and I was there because possibly, Joe Jones or somebody from Kansas City who had played with them, didn't, or couldn't make that date, and it took a lot of hello's and explanations -- nobody remembered that I was that kid in Kansas City, and I didn't get any credit on the album, that I was around at the time, so I fit in on that date, I put that badly. The arrangements were by Ernie Wilkins, and it was like Basie's little nine-piece band, the backgrounds that we played.

And I settled back and did that record date. But I have had hundreds and hundreds of musicians who have asked me what it was like because it is one of their favorite records. Now that record was reviewed two or three years later, in the New York Times, I believe it was, by a panel and a group of jazz critics; some of them prestigous -- and they picked 80, I believe I have the article someplace , we can't research it now, but they picked 80 of the foremost jazz records of all time, beginning way back, all down through the years,and this album was high on the list as a must for anybody's record collection and listening.
